title: Self Hosted Agentic AI: 2026 Guide to Setup and Costs
summary: Self hosted agentic AI software plans and acts across your tools on infrastructure you control.
body_markdown:
## Running the agent layer yourself with Activepieces


### Controlling what your agent touches


Activepieces lets you decide what your agent can touch, and it does so from an instance you host yourself.


It's an MIT-licensed automation core you run on Docker, Compose or Kubernetes, air-gapped if you need it, with agents that call your own models and apps. It doesn't host models, so that part stays yours.


The licence is a file you can read: the core is MIT, and the` packages/ee/` directories sit under a separate commercial licence in the repository's LICENSE file.


That boundary is the point. If the stack is already inside your network, the open question is which flows the agent can trigger, which credentials each step uses, and what gets written down afterward.


In a flow, every step is an explicit connection to one named app, drawn from the 740 integrations in the open source monorepo's` packages/pieces/community` directory, so the agent's reach is something you can read, not something you infer from a prompt.


The run detail view for an agent step lists each call to a tool as its own entry, with the input sent and the output returned, and the enterprise RBAC docs list app connections among the things an access policy governs for an agent, alongside SSO, SCIM and audit logs in the same enterprise feature set.


### Free trial and governance costs for self-hosted agents


Before anyone signs anything, you can test the whole arrangement on the free[Community](https://community.ibm.com/HigherLogic/System/DownloadDocumentFile.ashx?DocumentFileKey=6843edf1-f78a-c862-18f5-8fb659b4f004&forceDialog=0) edition, which self-hosts with unlimited runs.


For enterprise governance (SSO, SCIM, RBAC and audit logs), plus support for regulated or air-gapped deployments, you arrange it with the sales team at[https://www.activepieces.com/sales](https://www.activepieces.com/sales) .


Treat that as a real line in your plan: if you need per-team permissions or a formal audit trail, you're not on the free tier.


### Reading the run log


When something breaks, the run log is where this pays off. The screenshot below shows a failed step expanded on a self-hosted instance, with the exact input the agent sent and the output the app returned.


Read it as evidence: you can see whether the agent passed something it shouldn't have had, and whether the tool's response carried data that now sits in your logs.


Stored on your instance, those inputs and outputs are good for debugging and a liability for privacy. Whatever the agent handled is now in the log, so the log needs the same access controls as the systems it came from.


What Activepieces gives you is the place to look. It doesn't yet decide for you what should be redacted, and neither does MCP.
